title: Power BI Semantic Models in Microsoft Fabric: Storage Modes, Direct Lake, and Capacity Internals
summary: A practitioner's guide to semantic models in Microsoft Fabric and Power BI — what they are, how Import, DirectQuery, Composite, and Direct Lake modes differ, best practices for large models and row-level security, and the internal memory management mechanics that govern query performance.
body_md:
## What Is a Semantic Model?

A semantic model is the container of modeled data that Power BI reports, dashboards, and apps are built on, and a single semantic model can combine multiple data sources [S1]. The concept was previously called a "dataset"; the rename reflects its role as a fully modeled, Analysis Services–based structure rather than a raw data dump.

Every semantic model — apart from streaming models — is built on Analysis Services tabular modeling technology [S4]. That foundation means it inherits tabular's compression, DAX query engine, and XMLA endpoint, whether the model is tiny and hosted in a shared workspace or multi-terabyte and running on a Fabric capacity.

Semantic models hold data in a highly compressed in-memory cache by default, which is what makes interactive dashboards feel near-instant [S3]. Without the large storage format enabled, the default model size ceiling is 1 GB [S3].

---

## How Semantic Models Are Created

Models reach the Power BI service through several paths: publishing a Power BI Desktop file, uploading an Excel workbook or CSV, connecting to an externally hosted Analysis Services model, or creating push and streaming models through the REST APIs [S4].

One path that disappeared quietly: before September 5, 2025, creating a Fabric lakehouse would automatically generate a default semantic model. That auto-creation no longer happens, and any default models that existed prior to that date were decoupled from their parent lakehouses into fully independent semantic models by November 30, 2025 [S5].

---

## Storage Modes

![Power BI semantic model storage modes across Import, DirectQuery, Composite, and Direct Lake](/content/diagrams/semantic-model-storage-modes.svg)

Power BI Desktop exposes three storage modes — Import, DirectQuery, and Composite — defined by where the data lives at query time [S4].

### Import

Import mode copies data into the model's in-memory VertiPaq store. Queries run entirely in memory, which is fast, but the data is a snapshot: it only reflects the source as of the last refresh [S4]. An Import-mode model hosted in the service must be fully loaded into memory before it can answer any query [S4].

### DirectQuery

DirectQuery leaves data in the source and translates each DAX expression into a source query at runtime, so results always reflect the current state of the source system [S4]. The trade-off is query latency: every user interaction generates one or more source queries. Both Import and DirectQuery models require an on-premises data gateway whenever the source is not reachable directly over the internet [S4].

### Composite

Composite models mix Import and DirectQuery tables in a single model, letting designers cache stable, high-cardinality dimensions while keeping fast-changing fact data live [S4]. This is a middle path: some tables stay fresh at the cost of source load; others are fast at the cost of freshness.

### Direct Lake

Direct Lake is a fourth mode exclusive to Microsoft Fabric. A semantic model in Direct Lake mode loads columns from Delta tables stored in OneLake on demand, rather than importing or querying the source at query time [S6]. The model reads the Delta parquet files directly, so it is always pointing at the latest committed data without a scheduled refresh.

A Direct Lake–mode semantic model is consumed exactly like any other Power BI semantic model: it supports reports, explorations, and DAX queries with no special client-side handling [S2].

---

## Reports and the Live-Connection Model

Reports built on a published semantic model connect to it via a live connection, letting analysts author and edit reports without touching the model itself. Build permission on the model is the minimum required to live-connect [S2].

Live-connecting to a published model is distinct from live-editing that model inside Power BI Desktop, and also distinct from authoring a local model where Import or DirectQuery tables are bundled with the report file [S2]. Keeping the model and the report separate is the standard enterprise pattern: one model, many reports.

Report-level measures can be defined inside a live-connected report in Power BI Desktop, adding a private calculation to that report without writing anything back to the shared model [S2].

Beyond interactive reports, a semantic model also serves paginated reports, ad-hoc DAX queries (including the DAX query view), data explorations, and refreshable Excel pivot tables through the Analyze in Excel integration [S2].

When an organization already has significant Analysis Services investments, live-connecting to that existing model — either SQL Server Analysis Services or Azure Analysis Services — is the recommended approach rather than rebuilding the model inside Power BI [S4]. SSAS requires an on-premises gateway for the live connection; Azure Analysis Services does not. In both cases, the authenticated user's identity is forwarded to the external model to enforce data permissions [S4].

---

## Row-Level Security

Row-level security (RLS) roles in a semantic model work in two ways. Dynamic RLS filters each user's view based on their sign-in identity, typically using the `USERPRINCIPALNAME()` DAX function. Static RLS applies one fixed filter to every user assigned to the role [S4].

Changing gateway and cloud connection settings on a model requires ownership; non-owners see the model read-only. Ownership can be taken programmatically, which is useful when the original model owner leaves the organization [S4].

---

## Large Semantic Models

The large semantic model storage format lifts the 1 GB default ceiling to the size of the Fabric capacity itself, or to a maximum set by the capacity administrator. It is available on Fabric F SKUs, Premium P SKUs, Embedded A SKUs, and Premium Per User [S3].

The diagram below breaks that decision down further: how per-table storage mode is routed in a composite model, how dynamic versus static row-level security roles are chosen, the levers that drive capacity footprint, and where refresh memory risk emerges.

![Decision diagram: composite semantic model per-table storage-mode routing, RLS role decision, capacity-footprint levers, and refresh memory-risk internals](/diagrams/semantic-model-composite-decision.svg)

Note the upload boundary: the Power BI Desktop upload limit remains at 10 GB even with the large format enabled. A model exceeds that limit only inside the service, typically driven by an incremental refresh policy [S3].

### When to Enable the Large Format

Turn on the large semantic model storage format whenever XMLA-based tools will perform write operations against the model — even if the model is currently small — because the large format improves XMLA write performance regardless of model size [S3].

Once a workspace contains a large-format semantic model, it cannot be reassigned to a capacity in a different Azure region. Push semantic models cannot use the large storage format at all [S3].

### Estimating In-Memory Footprint

A model's in-memory footprint can be estimated from VertiPaq DMVs: sum the `DICTIONARY_SIZE` values from `DISCOVER_STORAGE_TABLE_COLUMNS` and the `USED_SIZE` values from `DISCOVER_STORAGE_TABLE_COLUMN_SEGMENTS`, queried over the XMLA endpoint using SQL Server Management Studio [S3].

---

## Best Practices

- **Live-connect, don't copy.** When an enterprise Analysis Services model already exists, reuse it through a live connection rather than recreating the model inside Power BI [S4].
- **Use report-level measures for report-specific logic.** Define measures in the report rather than the shared model when a calculation belongs only to one report, so the shared model stays lean [S2].
- **Enable the large storage format for XMLA write workloads.** Even a small model benefits from the large format if XMLA write tools (Tabular Editor, ALM Toolkit, etc.) are in the workflow [S3].
- **Lean on Direct Lake composites for mixed-freshness requirements.** Place very large fact tables in Direct Lake mode to avoid refresh cost, while placing smaller dimension tables in Import or DirectQuery within the same composite model [S7].
- **Right-size refresh granularity near the capacity memory ceiling.** Use the enhanced refresh REST API or the XMLA endpoint for fine-grained partition-level refreshes rather than full model refreshes when the model size is large [S3].
- **Tune capacity resource impact deliberately.** The main levers for capacity footprint are the model's hosting location, storage mode, gateway dependencies, imported data volume, and refresh type and frequency [S4].

---

## What Goes Wrong

**Running out of memory mid-refresh.** Refreshing a model whose size approaches half the capacity's memory — for example a 12 GB model on a 25 GB-memory capacity — risks exhausting memory during the refresh operation. The mitigation is to issue fine-grained refreshes through the enhanced refresh REST API or the XMLA endpoint rather than triggering a full model refresh [S3].

---

## Performance and Internals

The following section describes verified implementation details of the large semantic model storage format.

**Storage format change.** Enabling the large-format toggle changes the model's backend storage from ABF (Analysis Services Backup File) to Premium Files. This is why the feature is only available in Azure regions that support Azure Premium Files storage [S3].

**VertiPaq segment size.** Large-format models default to a VertiPaq segment size of 8 million rows, matching the Azure Analysis Services default. This size was chosen to balance memory consumption against query performance and to keep behavior comparable when migrating models from Azure Analysis Services [S3].

**Dynamic memory eviction.** The Fabric service uses dynamic memory management to evict inactive semantic models from capacity memory. This lets the combined size of all models in a capacity exceed the SKU's total memory. However, any single model is still bounded by the SKU memory limit, and a freshly evicted model incurs noticeable query latency when it must be reloaded [S3].

**On-demand load.** On-demand load, enabled by default for large-format models, pages only the relevant data pages into memory rather than loading the whole model at once. This makes previously evicted models answer queries again much faster than a full reload would require [S3].

**Temperature and access statistics.** With on-demand load active, the `DISCOVER_STORAGE_TABLE_COLUMN_SEGMENTS` DMV exposes per-column Temperature and Last Accessed statistics, revealing which columns are actually paged into memory and how the model's data is used in practice [S3].

**Import-mode full-load requirement.** An Import-mode model — regardless of size — must be fully loaded into capacity memory before it can serve any query. There is no partial load path for Import mode [S4].

---

## Worked Example: A Sales Analytics Model

Consider a retail organization with a 50 GB sales transaction history in OneLake (Delta format) and a set of small product and store dimension tables refreshed nightly from a warehouse.

*Inference:* A composite Direct Lake model is a natural fit. The fact table (`sales_transactions`) stays in Direct Lake mode, pointing directly at the Delta parquet files in OneLake. The dimension tables (`dim_product`, `dim_store`, `dim_date`) are small enough to import, which means dimension lookups never hit the source at query time.

Setup steps grounded in verified claims:
1. Create the semantic model and set the storage format to **large** immediately, because XMLA write tools will be used during development [S3].
2. Set `sales_transactions` to Direct Lake mode — it loads columns from the Delta table on demand without a scheduled refresh [S6].
3. Place dimension tables in Import mode within the same composite model to keep joins in-memory and avoid round-trips to the source for every filter interaction [S7].
4. Define two RLS roles: a dynamic role using `USERPRINCIPALNAME()` for regional managers (filters by region), and a static role for the board report (always sees national totals) [S4].
5. Publish the model to the workspace. Reports connect via live connection; report authors build views and local measures without touching the shared model [S2].
6. Monitor capacity memory usage via the `DISCOVER_STORAGE_TABLE_COLUMN_SEGMENTS` DMV. If the sales fact table's columns show low Temperature values, those columns are rarely queried and the effective in-memory footprint is much smaller than the full table size [S3].
7. Should a full refresh ever be needed, use the XMLA endpoint for partition-level refresh rather than triggering a full model refresh — especially if the model size approaches half the capacity's memory allocation [S3].
